163.history: The ford town east of the capital is where Rathad na Mèinne crossed the river before climbing into the hills. In the spring of the hundred and forty-ninth year Major Peter Ashdown turned his relief column north about An Taigh-seinnse Mòr to cross there, and met the crews of Baile thais dug in along the willow scrub of the far bank. His column went into the ford waist-high and in poor order, lost forty men to the river and the fire and all its baggage, and went back. The rebels lost nineteen, whose names the council's clerk read aloud once. The old field of battle at Muileann ghlas lies to its south-west. A' Chompanaidh's baggage abandoned on the near bank went up the hill road on the rebels' carts that night.

315.history: The low fort-city of the east, an hour's walk from the silver town, kept a small constable post from the years of the constables. Cut off by the rising, it yielded to Comann an Airgid's riflemen after a single exchange of fire, and the whole east of the island stood clear of human arms. The old walls of Talla na Lasrach stand at it, where the keeper of the flame once settled the silver quarrel of the guild by giving each side half.

10.history: The river town under the red cliffs on the Abhainn uaine lives on river fish and the short ferries between its two landings. In the first spring of the war the crew-leaders of the river towns met seven men in the back room of its inn, An Cupa Dàna, gave them sealed letters and hawks cast in lead from the cartridges of Muileann chrom, and sent them north to Oirthir an t-Seabhaig; they were Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe, and the boatman Coinneach Beag was among them. The ring of small river towns on the Abhainn uaine above Cathair mhòr heard the news of the war first at its inn fire, where word was turned over until everyone in the room had handled it.
10.known_for: the inn where Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe set out

166.history: The walled temple city of Òrd na Cloiche in the south-west declined in the first years to join the joint council of Baile dhìreach, a few miles off, its custodian writing that one town may be a trial but two would be a rule. In the war its priests heard Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe's letter and would send no men, since that was not what Òrd na Cloiche was for, but shut the harbour to A' Chompanaidh's ships and opened an Fhianna's roads to the hawk-faithful. Its temple of Lia Fàil, the stone that cries out, is the chief house of Òrd na Cloiche, and its priests keep a driftwood fire that burns blue-white with the salt.
166.known_for: the harbour shut in the war

63.history: The citadel harbour of the western coast was the humans' western port from the earliest years, and in the autumn of the hundred and fiftieth year it became the last seat of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach, when Strake came down the Abhainn gheal with his officers and clerks and the human families of the west and south came in behind its walls. It ran short of food within weeks, and Strake ordered A' Chompanaidh's store opened to humans and townsfolk alike at one measure, with no ledger kept. The last ship from an Tìr Thall anchored off it at Samhain. Its Dia-thìrich townsfolk kept their own houses and their own market cross through three generations of A' Chompanaidh's officers at the quay, and found themselves strangers in their own gates in the last autumn.
63.known_for: the last seat, and the last ship

304.history: The ancient ford in the north-west, on the edge of the country the humans first settled, is where the envoys of the council and of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach met in its meeting-house in the last week of an Dàmhair of the hundred and fiftieth year, with two scribes writing the same words in two hands, and agreed the truce: the humans to withdraw into the north-west under safe-conduct, and the towns of that country to be left standing. The meeting-house has a single long table down its middle, and both copies of the truce were signed at it on the third day.

412.history: The drovers' town at the bent ford was one of the two where Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise sank deep wells in the drought years, and they held. In the last weeks of the age its custodians stood at the ford and counted the columns over, family by family, from first light until past noon; it was the last count the Dia-thìrich made of the humans on Dia-thìr in the age. Its people are drovers, and the ford is crossed by the drove road north.

346.history: The drovers' village at the wide ford was the last stage before the northern country. The columns camped a night in its fields below the town with their fires strung along the hedgerow, and several of the humans asked the custodians the name of the place and wrote it down; a woman brought to bed under a hedge that night asked it twice and gave it to her child. It had been a gathering place for the drovers of the north since before the strangers came, and the fields where the columns camped were grazing again by the spring.

303.history: The red walled city of the north-west, the greatest town of that country, had lived under the humans' governance longer than any other on the island. The truce named it the place where the columns would be received, and its own Dia-thìrich folk were given the choice, at a gathering in the market square, of staying under the truce or going south. The roll set the two numbers side by side, and they were close. It was held by Dia-thìreach lords from An Aois Naomh, and the humans' magistrates sat in its hall for most of the age.
303.known_for: the choice put to its people

489.history: The great river port of the west, a short march north-east of Ros bheag, was where the company of the hawk-faithful mustered under Ìomhar Seabhag's eye in the early summer of the hundred and fiftieth year, and where the seven of Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe were told they were one company with one name. The company held the road between Ros bheag and the north-west for the rest of the war. It is the largest place on the island after the capital, and its barges run down the Abhainn naomh to Ros àrsaidh.
